problems.desc: Part (b): a correct sentence says that f(3) is an instruction to substitute 3 for x in the rule and evaluate, not a product of a quantity f with 3. Full credit for naming substitution as the operation; partial credit for saying only that f is the name of the function.

Part (b): a correct answer says the student kept the function name as if it were a factor, writing a g beside every term, instead of replacing the input variable x by 5. The letter naming the function never enters the arithmetic. Full credit for identifying the stray function name as the error; no credit for an answer that only recomputes the value.

Part (b): a correct answer says that the parentheses in f(2+3) hold the input, so the whole sum 5 is substituted once and squared, while f(2)+f(3) squares each number separately and adds the constant twice. Splitting across a plus sign is a distributive move, and substitution is not multiplication, so it is not allowed. Full credit for tying the failure to the parentheses holding an input rather than a factor.

traps.desc: read the notation as a product and divided 20 by 6 without undoing the subtraction

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct answer says the student treated the notation as a product of two quantities and divided, when the equation actually asks which input makes the rule output 20, so the rule must be undone term by term. Full credit for naming the false product step; partial credit for showing the correct solution with no diagnosis.

traps.desc: used only the per-shirt rate and dropped the fixed setup fee

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct answer states that 25 is the one-time setup charge in dollars, paid whatever the order size, and that the notation names the cost of an order of 4 shirts rather than four copies of some number. Full credit for both halves; partial credit for the meaning of the setup charge alone.

traps.desc: read the notation as a product set to zero and answered that the input is zero

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct answer says that a product being zero forces a factor to be zero, but the expression is not a product of two quantities: it is the amount of water left after t minutes, so setting it to zero asks when the tank empties. Full credit for rejecting the zero-product move by pointing out there is no product.

Part (c): a correct sentence says the first expression fixes the input at zero and asks for the output, while the second fixes the output at zero and asks for the input; one is an evaluation, the other is an equation to solve. Full credit for naming which quantity is given in each.

Part (b): a correct answer computes twice the value at input 3, gets 30, compares it with the value 48 at input 6, and says the two disagree, so doubling the input does not double the output. It then states that the notation instructs substitution of 6 into the rule, not multiplication of a quantity by 6. Full credit for the numerical comparison plus the statement about substitution.
